methods.label: Bound the number of files per disk
methods.explanation:
Since files cannot be split, consider how many whole files each disk can hold. We will rule out twelve disks and then find an arrangement using thirteen.

Even four of the smallest files require \(4(0.4)=1.6\) mb, exceeding the \(1.44\)-mb capacity. Thus a disk holds at most three files. Moreover, three files including a \(0.7\)-mb or \(0.8\)-mb file require at least
\[
0.7+0.4+0.4=1.5\text{ mb}>1.44\text{ mb}.
\]
Therefore, every disk holding three files must contain three \(0.4\)-mb files. There are only fifteen such files, so at most five disks can hold three files.

To bound the file count on twelve disks, allow two files per disk, then at most one extra file on each of the at most five three-file disks. The total is at most
\[
12(2)+5=29.
\]
This upper bound is less than thirty, so twelve disks cannot work. Fewer disks cannot work either, since adding empty disks would give an arrangement on twelve disks.

Thirteen disks suffice with the following arrangement:

- Three disks each hold one \(0.8\)-mb file and one \(0.4\)-mb file.
- Six disks each hold two \(0.7\)-mb files.
- Four disks each hold three \(0.4\)-mb files.

The disk loads are \(1.2\), \(1.4\), and \(1.2\) mb, respectively, all within capacity. This uses all three large files, all twelve medium files, and \(3+4(3)=15\) small files exactly once, on \(3+6+4=13\) disks. The minimum is \(\boxed{13}\), choice B.
